items.prompt: What is "cross-site scripting" (XSS)?
choices: Injecting attacker-controlled script into a page so it executes in another user's browser, in that user's own session
Sending unsolicited emails from a compromised server
Overwhelming a server with more requests than it can handle
Intercepting network traffic between two servers
items.explanation: XSS specifically involves attacker script executing in a victim's own browser session — not spam, denial of service, or network interception.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, whose browser actually executed the malicious script?
choices: Every other visitor's browser who viewed the page containing the comment, in their own logged-in session
Only the attacker's own browser, on their own machine
The web server's browser-based admin panel
No browser executed anything — the attack happened entirely on the server
items.explanation: The Scenario is explicit that the script ran in every visitor's browser, using their own session — that's the defining mechanism of XSS.

items.prompt: What is "cross-site request forgery" (CSRF)?
choices: Tricking a victim's already logged-in browser into submitting a request the victim didn't intend
Injecting a script that steals a user's password directly from a form
Guessing a user's password through repeated login attempts
Modifying a website's source code on the server directly
items.explanation: CSRF is specifically about forging an authenticated request via the victim's browser — not script injection, password guessing, or server-side code modification.

items.prompt: Per L1, does CSRF require injecting any code onto the vulnerable site?
choices: No — CSRF exploits the browser automatically attaching the victim's existing credentials to a request, without needing to inject any code
Yes — CSRF always requires injecting a script, exactly like XSS
Yes, but only a CSS injection, not a script injection
No, but only because CSRF exclusively targets mobile apps, not browsers
items.explanation: L1/L2 explicitly distinguish CSRF's mechanism (forged authenticated requests) from XSS's (code injection) — CSRF doesn't require injecting anything onto the vulnerable site.

items.prompt: What is "sanitization" in this unit's context?
choices: Ensuring user-supplied content is always treated as inert data when rendered, never interpreted as executable HTML or script
Removing all user-generated content from a website entirely
Encrypting user data before storing it in a database
Running a virus scan on uploaded files
items.explanation: Sanitization here specifically means preserving user content as inert data during rendering — not deleting content, encryption, or file scanning.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, what would sanitizing the comment's text have prevented?
choices: The `<script>` tag from being interpreted as executable markup when the page renders
The comment from ever being submitted to the server at all
Other users from being able to read the comment's visible text
The website's database from storing the comment
items.explanation: Sanitization specifically prevents malicious markup from being interpreted as code — it doesn't block submission, hide visible text, or prevent storage.

items.prompt: What is a "Content Security Policy" (CSP)?
choices: An HTTP header that tells the browser which sources of scripts and other resources are allowed to load and execute on a page
A company's internal policy document about handling sensitive data
A database access control list restricting which users can query which tables
A firewall rule blocking traffic from specific IP addresses
items.explanation: CSP is specifically a browser-enforced HTTP header restricting resource sources — not an internal policy doc, database ACL, or firewall rule.

items.prompt: Per L1, what role does CSP play relative to sanitization?
choices: It's a second, independent layer that limits the damage if an injection somehow still gets through, not a replacement for sanitizing input
It's the primary and only defense needed against XSS, making sanitization unnecessary
It's used exclusively to defend against CSRF, not XSS
It has no real relationship to XSS defense at all
items.explanation: L1 explicitly frames CSP and sanitization as complementary, independent layers — CSP is a safety net, not the primary or sole defense.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, did the attacker directly access any other user's account credentials?
choices: No — the attacker never touched any other user's account directly; the script ran using each victim's own existing session
Yes — the attacker used a leaked password database to log in as other users
Yes — the attacker directly guessed other users' passwords through repeated attempts
It's impossible to tell from the Scenario's facts
items.explanation: The Scenario's closing question is explicit that the attacker never touched other users' accounts directly — the exploit worked through the injected script alone.

items.prompt: What specifically did the injected script send to the attacker in the Scenario?
choices: Each visiting user's session cookie
The website's entire source code
A list of every other comment on the page
The server's database credentials
items.explanation: The Scenario describes the script sending each visitor's cookie to an attacker-controlled server — not source code, other comments, or database credentials.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, would sanitizing user input fix a CSRF vulnerability?
choices: No — sanitization stops injected code from executing, but CSRF doesn't involve injecting any code onto the vulnerable page at all
Yes — sanitization is described as an equally effective fix for both XSS and CSRF
Yes, but only if the sanitization function also checks the request's origin header
No, because sanitization is only relevant to database queries, not web pages
items.explanation: L2 explicitly states sanitization doesn't address CSRF, since CSRF's mechanism doesn't involve injecting code onto the page at all.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what does CSRF need from the victim that XSS doesn't necessarily require?
choices: The victim needs to be logged in and interact with (or load) something the attacker controls, rather than just viewing an injected script on the vulnerable site
The victim needs to manually enter their password into a fake login form
The victim needs to disable their browser's built-in security features
There's no real difference in what's required from the victim
items.explanation: L2's table specifically distinguishes CSRF's requirement (being logged in, interacting with attacker-controlled content) from XSS's (just viewing a page with the injected script).

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, what distinguishes "stored" XSS from "reflected" XSS?
choices: Stored XSS saves the malicious script to the site's own data, serving it to every visitor; reflected XSS requires tricking one specific victim into a crafted request
Stored XSS only affects mobile browsers; reflected XSS only affects desktop browsers
Stored XSS is always less severe than reflected XSS
There's no meaningful difference between the two — they're the same attack with different names
items.explanation: L2's diagram distinguishes the two by persistence and victim scope — stored affects every viewer, reflected requires one tricked victim per attack.

items.prompt: Per L2, is the Scenario's comment-based attack an example of reflected or stored XSS?
choices: Stored — the malicious comment is saved once and served to every subsequent visitor
Reflected — the script is part of a URL the victim was tricked into clicking
Neither — the Scenario doesn't fit either category
Both simultaneously — the comment is both stored and reflected at the same time
items.explanation: L2 explicitly classifies the Scenario as stored XSS, since the comment is saved and served to every visitor who views the page.

items.prompt: Per L2, if sanitization already prevents the injection, what does CSP add on top of that?
choices: A second, independent layer that can still block a script from executing or exfiltrating data, even if a sanitization bug lets it through
Nothing — CSP is described as entirely redundant once sanitization is in place
CSP replaces the need for sanitization entirely once configured
CSP only protects against CSRF, not against any XSS-related risk
items.explanation: L2 frames CSP as a genuinely independent safety net, not a redundant or replacement layer.

items.prompt: Per L2, does having a CSP mean sanitization can be safely skipped?
choices: No — CSP is a safety net for when the primary defense fails, not a substitute for sanitizing input in the first place
Yes — a correctly configured CSP makes sanitization entirely unnecessary
Yes, but only for sites that don't accept any user-submitted content
No, but only because most browsers don't fully support CSP yet
items.explanation: L2 explicitly rejects the idea that CSP alone is sufficient — sanitization remains the primary defense, with CSP as a backstop.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's wrong with treating XSS and CSRF as the same problem with one shared fix?
choices: Sanitizing displayed content does nothing to prevent a forged authenticated request, and a CSRF token does nothing to stop an injected script from executing
There's no real issue — a single shared fix is described as fully sufficient for both
This confusion only matters for sites without any user authentication
The issue is purely about naming conventions, not actual security coverage
items.explanation: L2 explicitly warns that each fix addresses a different mechanism — neither substitutes for the other.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's the risk of assuming only permanently stored input needs sanitizing?
choices: Reflected XSS shows that even data that's never permanently saved can still be dangerous if it's echoed back into a page unescaped
There's no risk — only stored input is ever actually dangerous
The risk only applies to sites using a specific database technology
This assumption is correct and is the recommended approach per L2
items.explanation: L2 explicitly warns against this assumption, using reflected XSS as the counterexample — unstored, echoed input is equally dangerous if unescaped.

items.prompt: Fix escapeHtml so it replaces all five structural HTML characters (&, <, >, ", ') with their literal text equivalents.

tests.description: a script tag is fully escaped, with no literal < remaining
the escaped output preserves the original text as literal characters
ampersands and quotes are also escaped correctly

items.explanation: Replacing the characters that give HTML its structural meaning with their literal text equivalents means a browser renders them as visible text instead of interpreting them as markup — the content is preserved exactly, but it can never be parsed as a tag.
items.reference:
❌ Raw insertion — user text becomes real HTML markup
✅ Escaped — structural characters become literal text, never parsed as a tag

Why: the browser can't tell trusted markup from injected markup once both are inserted the same way — escaping makes that distinction structural.

items.prompt: Fix escapeHtml so it replaces all five structural HTML characters (&, <, >, ", ') with their literal text equivalents.

tests.description: an image tag with an onerror handler is fully escaped, with no literal < remaining
quotes inside the string are escaped correctly
a single-quoted attribute-breakout attempt is escaped correctly

items.explanation: Same fix regardless of the specific injection attempt: replacing every structural character with its literal text equivalent closes the underlying mechanism, rather than trying to detect specific attack patterns.

items.prompt: Fix buildCspHeader so it joins each directive with its sources, and joins multiple directives with "; ".

tests.description: a single directive with one source
a single directive with multiple sources
multiple directives are joined with a semicolon and space

items.explanation: Mapping each directive to its space-joined source list, then joining every directive string with '; ', produces the exact header format browsers expect — each directive independently restricts what that category of resource is allowed to load from.
items.reference:
📜 Directive — a resource category, like script-src or img-src
🔗 Sources — the allowed origins for that category, space-separated

Why: CSP is enforced by the browser itself, independent of whatever sanitization the page's own code does.
